cases.note: The whole loan, once. `latest` names what was just published, the identity that comes back is the frame that went in, and the counters say one of each.

The case the six unit tests written with this reference could not see, because not one of them published twice into a pool with more than one slot. A pool exists so that a reader can hold a frame while capture keeps going, and the slot each publish lands in is the entire mechanism by which it does. Publishing into the *oldest released* slot spreads four frames over three slots and leaves the two most recent ones intact; taking the first slot that happens to be free instead puts all four in slot 0, which is a one-slot pool wearing a pool’s costume — and §47.4 already has a one-slot latest-wins channel, so that reading makes §47.6 a duplicate of the section above it.

How a policy actually holds a frame: `latest`, then `acquire` on what it named. Between those two calls capture publishes, which is not a race being tolerated — it is the ordinary case at any frame rate above the reader’s turnaround. With more than one free slot the publish must land somewhere else and the acquire must still succeed; landing on the slot `latest` just named refuses the reader its frame on nearly every cycle and reports it as `stale_handle`, which reads as a reader bug.
`latest` before anything is published is `null`. A zero frame is a measurement nobody took, and a policy handed one cannot tell it from a dark room.

One slot, reused. The generation advances, so the first handle now names a frame that is not there — and the refusal is `stale_handle` rather than the frame that took its place. Slot reuse is the normal case here, not the edge, which is why the generation is not optional.

cases.note: Every slot acquired, so the frame is dropped **and counted**. §47.4: capture is never stalled, because stalling capture to protect a slow reader starves the policy to protect the reader — the same error as starving the policy to protect the recording, one step over. The pinned frame is still the newest afterwards: the drop changed nothing a reader can see except the counter, which is where it belongs.
cases.expected: {"final":{"latest":{"generation":1,"slot":0,"stream":"head_rgb"},"stats":{"acquired":1,"dropped":1,"published":1,"released":0}},"steps":[{"handle":{"generation":1,"slot":0,"stream":"head_rgb"},"op":"publish"},{"identity":{"sequence":1,"stamp_ns":33333333,"stream":"head_rgb"},"op":"acquire"},{"op":"publish","refusal":{"code":"pool_exhausted","message":"Every slot is acquired, so frame 2 was dropped and counted rather than stalling capture."}},{"handle":{"generation":1,"slot":0,"stream":"head_rgb"},"op":"latest"},{"op":"stats","stats":{"acquired":1,"dropped":1,"published":1,"released":0}}]}

cases.note: A second acquire of a handle already checked out is refused by name, and so is a second release. Handles are single-owner loans rather than reference counts: a reader that cannot track its own loans is a reader whose next frame cannot be trusted either, and a double release would unpin a later loan taken on the same slot.
cases.expected: {"final":{"latest":{"generation":1,"slot":0,"stream":"head_rgb"},"stats":{"acquired":1,"dropped":0,"published":1,"released":1}},"steps":[{"handle":{"generation":1,"slot":0,"stream":"head_rgb"},"op":"publish"},{"identity":{"sequence":1,"stamp_ns":33333333,"stream":"head_rgb"},"op":"acquire"},{"op":"acquire","refusal":{"code":"already_acquired","message":"This handle is already checked out; a handle is one loan, not a share."}},{"op":"release","released":true},{"op":"release","refusal":{"code":"double_release","message":"This handle was already released; releasing it twice would unpin a later loan."}},{"op":"stats","stats":{"acquired":1,"dropped":0,"published":1,"released":1}}]}

cases.note: A frame from another stream, a slot this pool does not hold, and a handle carrying a different stream name. All three are refused before anything is read, because a pool that accepted a handle from a neighbouring stream would hand a policy the wrong camera.
cases.expected: {"final":{"latest":null,"stats":{"acquired":0,"dropped":0,"published":0,"released":0}},"steps":[{"op":"publish","refusal":{"code":"unknown_stream","message":"This pool holds head_rgb and was handed a frame from wrist_cam."}},{"op":"acquire","refusal":{"code":"unknown_slot","message":"The handle names a slot this pool does not hold."}},{"op":"release","refusal":{"code":"unknown_slot","message":"The handle names a slot this pool does not hold."}},{"op":"stats","stats":{"acquired":0,"dropped":0,"published":0,"released":0}}]}

cases.note: Two slots held, then both let go, then two more frames. The order the released slots come back in is the property: the one holding the older frame is reused first, so the newer of the two survives one more publish than it otherwise would. This is the same rule as `four-frames-into-three-slots` after a reader has been through, which is where an implementation that tracked "oldest" by slot index rather than by frame diverges.

The degenerate pool, which is a legal declaration rather than a mistake: a stream whose reader is always faster than capture needs no depth. Every publish reuses the one slot and the generation counts them, so a handle from three frames ago is refused rather than answered.
